Everyday life · 27 November 2026

Black Friday: what psychology knows about the buying mind

Scarcity, countdowns and crossed-out prices. Some well-studied mechanisms that explain why we buy more than we meant to, and how to pause in time.

Today is Black Friday. For a few days, shop windows and screens fill up with percentages, countdown clocks and "last few left" warnings. You do not have to be naive to end up buying something you had not planned: these techniques rely on mechanisms psychology knows well.

Scarce things seem better

In 1975 Stephen Worchel and colleagues offered biscuits to a group of participants. Some came in a jar holding ten and others in a jar holding only two. The same biscuits were rated as more desirable when there were few left, and even more so when the jar had been emptied in front of the participants. Robert Cialdini counted scarcity among the major principles of persuasion. "Only 3 left", "today only" and countdown timers all work on the same logic.

The crossed-out price

In 1974 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described anchoring: when we have to estimate a quantity, the first number we see pulls our answer towards it, even if it is arbitrary. A crossed-out original price acts as an anchor. Next to €199, €119 looks like a bargain, although the useful question is a different one: would I buy it for €119 on an ordinary Tuesday?

The fear of missing out

Kahneman and Tversky also showed that losses weigh more than equivalent gains, which is known as loss aversion. That is why many adverts do not talk about what you will gain by buying, but about what you will "miss" if you do not.

When shopping stops being fun

For most people, a one-off splurge ends as an awkward bill. But for some, shopping becomes a way of soothing sadness or anxiety, with loss of control, debt and family conflict. If that sounds familiar, it is worth talking to your family doctor or a mental health professional. Asking for help is not an overreaction.

Five simple brakes

  • Make a list before you look at offers and set a budget.
  • Ask yourself whether you would buy it at that price without the discount label.
  • Leave items in the basket for 24 hours before paying.
  • Turn off shop notifications for these few days.
  • Remember that almost every "last chance" comes back.

References

  1. Worchel, S., Lee, J. y Adewole, A. (1975). Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(5), 906–914.
  2. Tversky, A. y Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131.
  3. Kahneman, D. y Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263–291.
  4. Cialdini, R. B. (2009). Influence: Science and Practice (5.ª ed.). Boston: Pearson.
